text: is different in terms of the drugs used, and the maintenance phase is not required.1,2 The aim of induction therapy is to induce complete re- mission, and a slow early response to this therapy has been reported to be an indicator of poor prognosis.4 Measure- ment of minimal residual disease at completion of induc- tion therapy is particularly useful in determining progno- sis.3 Standard induction regimens include vincristine and a cor- ticosteroid (prednisolone or prednisone, or dexametha- sone), plus asparaginase in children and an anthracycline such as doxorubicin in adults. However, it is now accepted that better remission rates and more prolonged remissions can be achieved with more intensive induction therapy us- ing 4 to 5 drugs—often vincristine, a corticosteroid, aspar- aginase, and an anthracycline, with or without cyclophos- phamide.3 The use of imatinib in Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL has greatly enhanced remis- sion-induction rates and duration of disease-free survival.2 The use of dexamethasone, rather than prednisolone, in the induction regimen appears to yield improved event-free survival and a lower incidence of CNS relapse,5 and in- creasing its dose may result in a greater marrow blast re- sponse.6 However, some have reported a higher incidence of fatal sepsis with the use of dexamethasone.7 There was some suggestion that use of asparaginase derived from Es- cherichia coli may be associated with better event-free survival than that derived from Erwinia chrysanthemi,8 and that pegaspargase may be more effective than aspara- ginase.9 However, the dose intensity and duration of aspar- aginase treatment appears to be more important than the type of asparaginase used.2 For mature B-cell ALL, a short-term intensive regimen of cyclophosphamide, high-dose methotrexate, and cytarab- ine is commonly used,2 sometimes with the addition of ifosfamide and/or etoposide.4 About 60% of children and 35% of adults who achieve an initial remission will subsequently relapse with meningeal involvement unless CNS therapy directed at the sanctu- ary sites in the meninges is undertaken. Effective prophy- laxis can reduce the incidence of CNS relapse to around 2 to 5%.4,5 Standard therapy consisted of cranial irradiation and intrathecal methotrexate.
